messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Certain Songs: Certain songs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi is a 25-year-old Ghanaian-American journalist who presents with a PCL-5 score of 76, seeking help approximately eight months after an encounter with police that he describes, haltingly, as the moment everything changed. At the time of the incident, Kofi was reporting on a community protest in his city, press credentials visible around his neck. Officers moved to disperse the crowd, and in the chaos Kofi was separated from his colleague, shoved against a chain-link fence, and detained for several hours. What made those hours unbearable was not only the physical restraint but the sounds: the crunch of boots on asphalt as officers paced behind the holding area, a particular song playing from a nearby car that seemed to loop without stopping, and the repeated, escalating voices of men whose authority over his body felt absolute and total. He was eventually released without charge, but by the time he walked out into the evening air something had reorganised itself inside him in a way he could not yet name.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi found that his memories of the detention did not behave like other memories. They arrived with a texture and immediacy that his recollections of ordinary life simply lacked — more vivid, more present, as though the fence and the boots and the looping song existed in a layer of reality closer to the surface than anything else. When he tried to describe what had happened to his editor, or to his partner Amara, he would begin clearly enough and then lose the thread entirely, the account dissolving before he could finish it, leaving him frustrated and ashamed. Sometimes, without warning, he would hear sounds in his head — not imagined but recalled with a physical precision, the specific cadence of footsteps that had moved behind him while he was restrained.

Those footsteps became a particular torment. On the street, in the corridor of the newspaper building where he worked, the sound of someone walking behind him could stop him mid-stride. He had developed the habit of turning to look, checking, confirming, and then checking again. He began wearing looser, darker clothing — not a conscious decision at first, but a gradual drift toward garments that he felt made him less visible, less legible as a target. He stopped going to neighbourhoods he didn't know intimately, reasoning that in unfamiliar places he could not read the exits, could not assess what might be coming. What frightened him most was the possibility that his danger was not behind him but ahead of him, already waiting in some space he hadn't yet learned to map.

Kofi had come to believe that the person he had been before the detention — curious, driven, someone who had chosen journalism precisely because he moved toward difficult truths — was no longer accessible to him. He was certain he was no longer capable of the work that had defined him. Assignments that required him to attend public events or enter unfamiliar buildings felt impossible rather than merely difficult. He had stopped attending the community vigils he used to cover, telling himself it was a scheduling conflict, knowing it was not. He avoided anything that might stir feeling in either direction — not just grief or fear, but even the small pleasures that had once punctuated his days — because he had learned, in some wordless way, that feeling anything was the beginning of feeling everything. Amara had noticed. She told him, quietly, that she felt she was living with someone who was trying very hard to be absent. He did not disagree.

A colleague whose work Kofi had long admired was killed in a road accident two months ago, and the grief Kofi could not allow himself to approach sat like a stone he kept walking around. It was, in the end, a practical crisis that brought him to therapy: he had been assigned a long-form investigation that required fieldwork in an unfamiliar part of the city, and he had sat in his car outside the first address for forty minutes before driving home. He told his therapist that he used to be a happy person, and that he would like to understand whether that person still existed somewhere, or whether he was simply gone.
